All right, so on the screen in front of you, you see an example of two different traders labeled trader A and trader B. Both traders have a $10,000 account and both traders are risking $2 per pip on their account. Trader A is trading one target, 20,000 unit lot per trade, which is equal to somewhere around $2 per pip. If trader A makes 5,000 pips, then trader A is roughly going to make $10,000. Now, trader B is trading two target system. So, he is trading two 10,000 unit position sizes, which means for each position, for each trade, he's going to make $1 per pip. So, his same 5,000 pips will only produce him with $5,000. So, what does this mean? This means that if you're going to trade two targets on any strategy, then your two target system must at least make twice as many pips as a one target system in order to make the same amount of money. So your second targets must at least produce the same amount of pips as your first targets in order for you to be even with someone just trading one target. And in some strategies, this is very easy to accomplish. In other strategies, this is very difficult to accomplish. So to go into this in a little further detail, I've drawn another example here to the right. And as you can see here, same thing, $10,000 account, trader A trading one target. Trader B trading two targets. As you can see here to our target one labeled in green here is going to be 80 pips. Our target two here is 120 pips. So let's take trader A example first. Trader A has chose to short the market in trend continuation here making lower lows and lower highs. He's decided to short the market here and expectation for the market to continue down and put his stop loss above the swing high here. So trader A has a possibility to make 80 pips while risking 60. So once the market does come down and hit his target, trader A makes $160. Trader A risked $120 in order to make that $160. So he has still got over a 1:1 riskreward. Now let's look at trader B. In this example, trader B decided to take second targets at a 127 extension of the previous swing high to swing low, which is a common place to take second targets. pen for trader B. If this situation happened exactly as he assumed and the market did continue down, breaking through the previous low and hitting his second target, then he would have the upper hand on trader A, making $200 in his trade overall while risking the same 120. Now, the reason trader B is making 200 is because he's trading two 10,000 unit positions at $1 per pip. And his target one was $80 or 80 pips. His target two was $120 or 120 pips. So, for trader B, this situation gives him the upper hand of making $200 versus trader A's 160. Now the reason that it is very important to test for multiple targets on any of the strategies that you decide to trade is because the market does not always continue in trend does it? Sometimes we will see something like this in the market. And in this case, trader A has made his $160 hitting target one and he's out of the trade completely. Trader B has made $80, $1 per pip on his 80 pip win here. And he is still in the trade. At this point, he's moved his stop loss to break even to keep from losing any of the pips that he made on his first target. And now he's expecting the market to continue down and make another 120 pips or $120 for his account. but instead the market decides to reverse here and continue up instead of down, which it often does. So in this case, trader B has only made $80 versus trader A's 160 and trader B was still risking the same $120 as trader A. So, not only does trader B have a inverted riskreward, trader B also because of taking two targets has made less money on the specific trade. So, if you are going to decide to use two targets in a strategy, then you need to make sure to test over a long period of time to see if trading two targets is actually making your strategy more profitable or less profitable. Because in order for this strategy to be more profitable with multiple targets, then this second target must be hit very often. If you're only hitting second targets, now all this is of course depending on where your second targets are. Some people may choose to take second targets at a 1618 or previous structure. So all of that can definitely change the outcome of the trades. But for example sake, if you were to only hit this 127 20% of the time, then you may only do just as good as you could with one target. And so at that point, you're actually putting forth more effort in order to manage the position and roll stops to break even once first targets are hit with no extra income coming in from that extra effort. But if you hit your second targets 50% of the time, 40% of the time, then you're going to make more pips because of that. So, are multiple targets really better than single targets? That is completely determined by the strategy you're using? And the only way to determine whether or not that is the case is by testing that strategy over time throughout the market's history in order to see whether or not taking multiple targets has produced you with more or less profit throughout time. already at the trading channel and i'll be right back to tell you everything you need to know about the rsi indicator [Music] welcome back and let's go ahead and get started with what is the rsi indicator rsi actually stands for relative strength index and this indicator can be found on tradingview and in most platforms by going to your indicators and just typing in rsi and then looking for a relative strength index just in case you didn't know how to do that and this indicator uses historical price to help us determine directional strength of whatever market we are looking at for example if the euro yen which is the currency pair we are on right now has directional strength to the upside then we will see an rsi above 50. and i'm gonna explain why that's the case in just a second if we have directional strength to the downside then the rsi indicator will be below this little 50 line we can also use the rsi indicator to help us spot reversals but more on that a little bit later in the video now let's move on to how this indicator actually works so the math behind the formula for the rsi indicator can get a bit complicated it's important for you to understand that you don't need to know this formula or be able to solve it out you don't need to be a mathematician to use the rsi indicator and you not knowing the formula will affect your trades absolutely none but i do want to go over a brief overview of how the rsi is calculated in a very simple way simply put the rsi indicator looks at the last 14 candles and why is it the last 14 by the way it's the last 14 because that is the look back period or length that we have our rsi set to so whatever this is set to that's how many candles it looks at the rsi takes a look at the last 14 candles and it gets the average gain of the last 14 candles by adding up all the green candles and dividing that by the number of green candles that's how you get an average and then it takes that and it also looks at the average losses of the last 14 candles by adding the losses up for every red candle and then dividing that by the number of red candles if the average amount of gain is above the average amount of loss then we have an rsi above 50. that is a very simplistic way of understanding what the rsi is doing but that's how it works there are a couple of different ways to use the rsi indicator to find profitable trades and one of those is looking for reversals using this indicator that's what we're going to go over first because it is by far the most popular way to use the rsi so here on the rsi you can see a red line
